result: Spatial attention causes pRF shifts that occur primarily in the radial dimension (toward or away from the fovea) rather than horizontal or vertical directions. This radial shift pattern is consistent across the visual hierarchy, with shift magnitude increasing in higher visual areas. The apparent dominance of horizontal over vertical shifts is explained by overrepresentation of the horizontal meridian in visual field coverage.
evaluation: Claims C44-C52 provide converging evidence from visual inspection (C44, C45), statistical analysis (C46, C47, C48), and comparison to shift hypotheses (C48, C50) that pRF shifts occur radially. The explanation for horizontal dominance (C51, C52) is supported by both citations and data analysis. The statistical tests show p < 0.01 for radial vs horizontal shifts across ROIs.

result: Spatial attention produces eccentricity-dependent changes in pRF properties: parafoveal pRFs shift away from the fovea and increase in size, while peripheral pRFs shift toward the fovea and decrease in size. These changes in pRF eccentricity and size are strongly correlated (R = 0.74-0.99, p < 0.001) across all ROIs.
evaluation: Claims C53-C60 describe a coherent pattern of pRF changes with strong statistical support. The correlation between size and eccentricity changes (C59) is robust across ROIs. The pattern is consistent with the resolution hypothesis of attention and is replicated across individual ROIs (C54, C55, C57, C58).

result: An attentional gain field model parsimoniously explains the complex pattern of pRF shifts across visual regions. The model uses similar attentional gain field sizes across ROIs to capture widely varying eccentricity change profiles, demonstrating that differences in pRF shift patterns depend on differential spatial sampling properties rather than differing attentional influences.
evaluation: Claims C61-C67 demonstrate that the gain field model accurately reproduces observed data (C61), captures variation across ROIs with similar parameters (C62), and extends prior models to dynamic attention (C66). The model provides a mechanistic explanation (C63, C64) and confirms that attentional gain field precision is similar across the visual hierarchy (C67).

result: Attending to color produces stronger pRF changes compared to attending temporal frequency, with feature AMI around 0.05 on average (roughly 10% stronger changes) and reaching 0.20 in some ROIs (roughly 50% stronger changes). This effect is significant across all ROIs (p < 0.01).
evaluation: Claims C36 and C68-C72 provide consistent evidence for stronger pRF modulations when attending color. The feature AMI measure combines eccentricity and size changes into a robust index (C69), and statistical tests confirm significance across all ROIs (C70). Effect sizes are quantified (C71, C72).

result: Feature-based attentional modulations occur globally throughout visual cortex and do not depend on bottom-up feature preference. Despite large variations in feature preference between MT+/V1 (preferring temporal frequency) and VO/hV4 (preferring color), average feature AMI was nearly equal across these regions (R = 0.20, p = 0.608).
evaluation: Claims C37 and C76-C78 demonstrate independence of feature AMI from feature preference through lack of correlation (C77) and equal AMI across regions with different preferences (C76). The data replicate known feature specializations (C74, C75), confirming that the lack of correlation is not due to measurement error.

result: The greater spatial resampling when attending color can be explained by color being sampled by relatively smaller pRFs. This is supported by known differences in processing between parvocellular (color, fine-grained) and magnocellular (temporal frequency, coarse) pathways, differences in pRF size between MT+ and hV4, and eccentricity-dependent relationships between pRF size and color preference.
evaluation: Claims C79-C86 provide a mechanistic explanation linking behavioral predictions (C79, C80) to neural properties. The explanation is supported by established knowledge about visual pathways (C82), regional differences (C83), eccentricity dependence (C84, C85), and observed data (C85, C86). The logic is internally consistent.

result: The stronger influence of spatial attention when attending color is realized by a more precise attentional gain field at the stimulus location. Fitted stimulus attentional gain field sizes were significantly smaller when attending color compared to temporal frequency (0.094 dva smaller in combined ROI, t(4) = 9.021, p = 0.001, Cohen's d = 4.511).
evaluation: Claims C87-C92 provide a complete mechanistic account. The mathematical property of Gaussian multiplication (C87) leads to a testable prediction (C88) that is confirmed by modeling results (C89, C90). The control analysis (C91) ensures the effect is specific to the stimulus gain field. Effect sizes are large (Cohen's d > 2).

result: Spatial and feature-based attention interact such that resampling depends on both attended location and feature. This interaction occurs similarly throughout visual cortex regardless of feature preference, but depends on spatial sampling properties of voxels preferring the attended feature. The attentional system adjusts its influence according to spatial sampling characteristics of feature-preferring units.
evaluation: Claims C3-C7 and C93-C94 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing findings from multiple analyses. The interaction is demonstrated by feature AMI analysis (supporting C3), independence from regional feature preference (supporting C4), relationship to pRF properties (supporting C5), and gain field modeling (supporting C6). The conclusions are well-supported by the data.

result: Eye tracking and behavioral analyses demonstrate that pRF differences between conditions cannot be explained by fixation accuracy or task difficulty. Gaze position showed no difference between conditions (BF = 18620 for null), and the Quest procedure successfully equated performance across conditions (BF = 6.25 for null).
evaluation: Claims C98-C102 provide important control analyses using Bayesian statistics. The Bayes Factors strongly support the null hypothesis for gaze position (C98) and behavioral performance (C101). While gaze variability differed (C99), it did not differ between attention conditions (C100), ruling out confounds.

result: Individual differences in pRF shift patterns between subjects are well captured by the attentional gain field model and likely result from known individual differences in baseline pRF parameter distributions rather than different attentional mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C95-C96 address reproducibility across subjects. The model's ability to capture individual differences (C95) and the attribution to baseline pRF distributions (C96) are supported by the data and citations. This strengthens confidence in the main findings.

result: The study included five participants (two female, two authors, aged 25-37) with informed consent and ethical approval. Behavioral difficulty was equated across conditions using a Quest staircase procedure.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43 describe basic methodological details that are clearly stated and appropriate. The sample size is consistent with dense sampling approaches in fMRI. The Quest procedure for equating difficulty is standard and appropriate.

result: Summary of main findings: Spatial attention alters pRF eccentricity and size in concert, explained by an attentional gain field model. Attending color induces stronger changes than attending temporal frequency, occurring globally throughout the brain. This is related to smaller pRF sizes in color-preferring voxels and caused by a more precise attentional gain field.
evaluation: Claims C103-C109 summarize the main findings in the Discussion. These are restatements of results already evaluated above and are well-supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

result: The findings are consistent with previous studies showing attention-induced pRF changes, but provide new insights: pRFs shift radially (not just horizontally), with parafoveal pRFs shifting outward and peripheral pRFs shifting inward. This supports the resolution hypothesis of attention.
evaluation: Claims C120-C124 contextualize findings within prior literature. The consistency with prior work (C120) and novel insights (C121-C123) are supported by the data. The interpretation regarding the resolution hypothesis (C124) is reasonable given the pattern of results.

result: The attentional gain field model extends to situations with dynamically deployed attention and implements comparable gain field sizes across visual regions. However, the model did not capture decreases in pRF eccentricity of the most foveal pRFs in V1.
evaluation: Claims C126-C129 discuss model contributions and limitations. The extension to dynamic attention (C126) and comparable gain field sizes (C127) are supported by the modeling results. The limitation regarding V1 (C129) is honestly reported and discussed in relation to suppressive surrounds.

result: Feature-based attention modulates spatial attention's effects on spatial resampling globally throughout the brain, including early visual regions. While voxel-level measurements cannot distinguish between changes in individual neurons versus differential weighting of subpopulations, prior single-neuron studies support that spatial attention influences individual neuron sampling.
evaluation: Claims C111-C112 summarize key contributions that are well-supported by the data. The limitation acknowledged in C113 is important and appropriately qualified by citing single-neuron evidence (C114). This demonstrates appropriate caution in interpretation.

result: Prior to this study, no research had investigated the effect of feature-based attention on spatial sampling, though behavioral studies suggested that feature-based attention should influence spatial resampling to optimize sampling of attended features. The hypothesis tested is that attending color versus temporal frequency should lead to stronger spatial resampling.
evaluation: Claims C27-C29 and C34 establish the novelty and rationale of the study. The literature review (C27) and hypothesis derivation (C28-C29, C34) are appropriate. The hypothesis is clearly stated and testable.

result: The authors predict that results should generalize to any comparison of attended visual features that differ in spatial scale, including high versus low spatial frequency or faces versus letters.
evaluation: Claim C110 is a prediction for future work. While the logic is reasonable based on the current findings, this has not been tested. The prediction is appropriately framed as speculation but requires empirical validation.

result: The global pattern of pRF shifts could be caused by object-based attentional transfer, though the authors favor an interpretation of temporally dynamic but spatially consistent adaptation. The inferior frontal junction (IFJ) is suggested as a possible candidate for controlling interactions between feature-based and spatial attention.
evaluation: Claims C115-C116 and C119 are speculative interpretations. While C115 and C119 are appropriately framed as possibilities, they lack direct evidence from the current study. C116 is a reasonable interpretation but alternative explanations are not fully ruled out.

result: The functional implication of pRF size changes has been questioned, as stimulus encoding fidelity was shown to be unaffected by pRF size changes in a recent study.
evaluation: Claim C125 appropriately cites prior work (Vo et al., 2017) that questions the functional significance of pRF size changes. This is an honest acknowledgment of uncertainty in the field regarding interpretation of pRF size changes.

result: Prior studies showed that in early visual areas, spatial attention shifted pRFs away from the attended location, while in higher areas pRFs shifted toward the attended location. Other studies showed that in early visual regions, both pRFs and attentional gain fields have suppressive surrounds.
evaluation: Claims C130-C131 accurately cite prior research to contextualize the model limitation noted in C129. The citations are appropriate and relevant to the discussion of why the model may not capture foveal V1 pRF shifts.
